summary: A short 16-minute manager 1-1, cut off early because Richard had a call in seven minutes. It opens on the fallout from the Tyler Kirkwood call two days earlier: the $100 deposit was taken, the follow-up meeting was a no-show, and Chris coaches the exact two-message recovery sequence to send, why both messages must go together, and to refund the deposit if asked. He instructs Richard to re-review his own call for any moment of pushing rather than meeting. The rest is operational: calendar management across closers, double bookings, lead reassignment, a no-show call-and-text cadence, and how to use the setter as a second bite at a prospect after the closer call. Chris explicitly names the good cop / bad cop split between setter and closer.
notable: The $100 deposit taken from Tyler Kirkwood on 06/23 did not convert — the prospect no-showed the rescheduled call and went silent. Richard: 'I got them to deposit, I got them to commit, that I didn't show up.'

Chris treats a $100 deposit as a normal accountability device — 'I just gave this guy a hundred bucks to hold me accountable, and he's holding me accountable' — three days after telling the same rep that the deposit threshold for booking onboarding is $500 with $1,200 due before it runs.

Stated refund practice and its motive: 'Then you just say, no worries, I'll go ahead and send it over to you. Just out of curiosity, what changed?' and 'You want to send the money back because you never know with people, they might try to do a chargeback because they're afraid of being sold.'

Chris scripts the recovery message and flags its risk himself: 'the reason I say, have you given up on this... it definitely pierces right into it, the root of what's going on... But you've got to be careful with that language, because you don't want it to turn into shame.' The neutralising second message is 'no worries either way. Just let me know so we can either reschedule or I can send you back the deposit.'
Chris instructs a self-audit of the call for pressure: 'you review it just to see, was there any moment where it felt like you were pushing versus meeting?'

Setter used as a second approach after the closer call, with an explicitly staged dynamic: 'you can just play good cop, bad cop, because the closer is kind of the bad cop, because they're the one asking for the money. The setter is like the good cop.' The scripted opener is 'hey, just curious, how did the call go with John?' followed by probing payment plan options, and Chris says 'I can't tell you how many times I've saved the deal being the setter.'

Lead prioritisation instruction based on country: 'Alan doesn't really have a great app, Taz also doesn't really have a great app, but Alan is from the US, so I would prioritize Alan over Taz. That's the way I always look at it.'
Leads are reassigned between closers without the prospect being told — 'He didn't cancel it, I reassigned it over to you' — and this produced the double booking that made the Alan call happen.
Confirms the setter code convention: Richard asks 'he only said if it's KFS or something in the booking link, right?' and Chris answers 'That's Kim's initials, yep.'
No-show cadence stated: call two minutes past, text, call again at five, text again, stay in the room until ten past, then move to follow-ups. 'never, ever, ever count a lead out.'

An additional overflow closer is joining with a maximum of three slots at any time and lowest calendar priority; Chris says 'I've worked with him for many years'. RCA and Cole Gordon's team are again cited as the benchmark.
Recording disclosure was made, though the diarization attributes it to the wrong speaker: 'meeting is being recorded.'
